lead: A phase-locked loop (PLL) makes an oscillator follow the frequency of an input signal. It compares the phase of a voltage-controlled oscillator (VCO) with the incoming signal and adjusts the oscillator until the two match. The loop is used to demodulate FM, to multiply a frequency by an integer, and to recover a clock from serial data. This chapter explains the four blocks, the VCO formula f_out = f_0 + K_vco V_c, and the capture and lock ranges.
prereq: You need: Chapter 7.6 for a 555-based VCO, and Unit 4 for oscillator feedback and free-running frequency.

sections.h3: Four blocks in a closed loop

blocks.text: The input signal and the VCO output both enter the phase detector. The detector produces an error voltage proportional to their phase difference: V_e = K_pd (θ_in − θ_out). K_pd is the detector gain in volts per radian; θ_in and θ_out are the phases in radians.

The loop filter is a low-pass filter. It removes the sum-frequency term from the detector and passes the slowly varying error. It sets the loop's speed and stability. Its output is the control voltage V_c.

The VCO is an oscillator whose frequency is set by V_c. The feedback path returns the VCO output to the detector. If the VCO is slower than the input, the phase error grows in one direction; the detector and filter push V_c until the VCO speeds up.

items: Compare input and VCO phase; the detector gives an error voltage.
Low-pass filter the error to get V_c.
The VCO frequency shifts by K_vco V_c.
Feedback corrects until the two frequencies match.

blocks.text: In lock, the VCO frequency equals the input frequency. The phase error settles to a constant value. In a simple first-order loop, a steady phase error is needed to hold a non-zero V_c; in an ideal integrator (type-II) loop, the filter can hold V_c with zero steady phase error. The steady offset in the first-order case is the static phase error.

sections.h3: VCO line and the two ranges

blocks.where: f_out is the output frequency in Hz; f_0 is the free-running frequency in Hz when V_c = 0; K_vco is the VCO gain in Hz/V; V_c is the control voltage in V.

blocks.text: The relation is linear over a limited range. Outside it the VCO saturates and the loop cannot lock. For the 565 PLL the free-running frequency is set by one resistor and one capacitor: f_0 = 1.2 / (4 R_1 C_1). R_1 is in ohms, C_1 is in farads, and f_0 is in hertz. The 4046 is a CMOS PLL with an XOR phase detector and a VCO; its frequency is also set by external R and C.

The capture range is the band of input frequencies over which an unlocked loop can acquire lock. It is narrow and roughly set by the loop bandwidth, which depends on the loop filter and the loop gain. The lock range is the wider band over which a loop that is already locked keeps lock. So lock range > capture range. Lock time is the time taken to acquire lock.
FM demodulation: the FM input drives the PLL. The VCO follows the instantaneous input frequency, and V_c is a copy of the modulating message.

Frequency multiplication: put a divider by N in the feedback path. The loop forces the divided output to equal the input, so f_out = N f_in. A 10 kHz reference and a divider by 8 give a 80 kHz output.

Clock recovery: serial data has transitions at the bit rate but no separate clock. The PLL locks to those transitions and its VCO output becomes the clock. The same idea times read channels in disks and receivers in digital links.

figure.caption: The phase detector compares the input with the fed-back VCO output; the loop filter turns the error into V_c, which sets the VCO frequency. Notice the feedback path from VCO to detector.

spec.title: PLL blocks
spec.aria: An input signal and the fed-back VCO output enter the phase detector; the loop filter turns the error into V_c, which sets the VCO frequency. The VCO output is also the output f_out.

examples.question: A 565 PLL has R_1 = 12 kΩ and C_1 = 2.5 nF. (a) Find its free-running frequency. (b) The VCO gain is 6 kHz/V. Find the output frequency for V_c = +0.5 V. (c) State whether the loop locks to a 13 kHz input that lies inside the capture range.
steps: Compute the time constant: 4 R_1 C_1 = 4 × 12 × 10³ × 2.5 × 10⁻⁹ = 1.2 × 10⁻⁴ s.
Frequency shift: Δf = K_vco V_c = 6 kHz/V × 0.5 V = 3 kHz.
Output frequency: f_out = 10 kHz + 3 kHz = 13 kHz.
The 13 kHz input is inside the capture range, so the loop acquires lock and holds it with V_c ≈ 0.5 V.
examples.answer: f_0 = 10,000 Hz (10 kHz); f_out = 13,000 Hz (13 kHz); the loop locks to the 13 kHz input because it lies inside the capture range.
examples.check:
R1 = 12e3
C1 = 2.5e-9
f0 = 1.2 / (4 * R1 * C1)
Kvco = 6e3
Vc = 0.5
fout = f0 + Kvco * Vc
print(f0)
print(fout)

traps: Swapping capture range and lock range: capture is the narrower band where an unlocked loop can acquire lock; lock is the wider band where it holds lock.
Expecting lock on an input far outside both ranges: the VCO cannot reach that frequency with the available control voltage.
Mixing units: K_vco in kHz/V times V_c in volts gives kHz; add that to f_0 in kHz, not to f_0 in Hz.
Thinking the loop filter is just any low-pass: its cut-off sets capture range, lock time and stability.
Confusing the free-running frequency f_0 with the input frequency: f_0 applies when V_c = 0.

quiz.q: Define the free-running frequency of a VCO.
quiz.a: The output frequency when the control voltage is zero, written f_0.

quiz.q: Why is a low-pass filter placed after the phase detector?
quiz.a: It removes the sum-frequency component and high-frequency noise, leaving the slowly varying error that becomes V_c.

quiz.q: A VCO has f_0 = 20 kHz and K_vco = 5 kHz/V. Find f_out for V_c = 0.8 V.
A 565 has R_1 = 15 kΩ and C_1 = 1 nF. Find f_0.
A loop is locked at 100 kHz. The input moves to 104 kHz. With K_vco = 8 kHz/V, what change in V_c holds lock, if the loop filter can supply it?
How does a divider by N in the feedback path multiply the input frequency?
quiz.a: The divider output is f_out/N. The loop forces this to equal f_in, so f_out = N f_in.

quiz.q: Why can a PLL fail to lock to an input far outside both capture and lock ranges?
quiz.a: The VCO cannot reach that frequency with the available control voltage, so the phase error never settles and the loop stays unlocked.

beyond: Not for the exam. Practical PLLs use charge-pump phase detectors and current-controlled oscillators; fractional-N dividers allow non-integer multiplication for radio synthesizers. Jitter and phase noise decide whether a recovered clock is clean enough for high-speed links. Search 'charge-pump PLL', 'fractional-N frequency synthesizer' and 'PLL phase noise' to go further.
